subject: Climate & Environment
title: Rising Global Temperatures
description: A 60-second lesson on Rising Global Temperatures.

hook.text: Earth has warmed about 1.1°C since the 1800s. That sounds small. It isn't.

buildup.text: During the last ice age, the planet was only about 6°C cooler than today.

discovery.text: Small global averages hide extremes — the Arctic has warmed four times faster.

twist.text: The hottest years on record have all occurred since 2010.

climax.text: At 1.5°C, heat waves double. At 2°C, some regions become unlivable in summer.

punchline.text: A degree on a thermometer is a disaster on a planet.

quiz.question: How much has Earth warmed since the 1800s?

details.summary: Global average surface temperature has risen roughly 1.2 degrees Celsius since pre-industrial times. The warming is not uniform: the Arctic warms two to four times faster, land warms faster than oceans, and nights warm faster than days.
details.whyItMatters: The 1.2-degree average masks more extreme regional warming. Understanding the pattern reveals why some areas are already experiencing climate impacts far beyond the global mean.
takeaways: Earth has warmed about 1.2 degrees Celsius since the 1850s
The Arctic is warming two to four times faster than the global average
The 10 warmest years on record have all occurred since 2010

faq.question: Why does a 1.2-degree average matter if daily variation is much larger?
faq.answer: A small shift in the average moves the entire distribution of weather events. This means extreme heat waves that were once rare become common, glaciers melt year-round, and ecosystems face sustained stress rather than brief temperature swings.

faq.question: Why does the Arctic warm faster than the rest of the planet?
faq.answer: As ice melts, it exposes darker ocean and land that absorb more sunlight, creating a feedback loop called Arctic amplification. Less ice means more absorption, which means more warming, which melts more ice.
